title: Values that stay and values that change

outcomes.can: Predict the order and values printed after a numeric update.
Declare a numeric variable with an inferred type and calculate the number remaining.
Use a fixed text binding and combine supplied text in order.
Identify a number assigned to a text variable and repair the numeric count.
Preserve a starting value when calculating a changed value in another setting.

intro: A task board starts the day with some open tasks. When more arrive, its count changes. How can a program keep the original count and show the new one?

steps.title: Give a value a name
steps.text: A value is a piece of data. 4 is a number. "Desk" is text (a string). true and false are the two boolean values. A variable is a name for a value. const opening = 4 gives a fixed name its first value. let open = opening gives a second name the same number and allows us to assign it a new value later. Read = as “gets.” A semicolon ends a statement. The program runs these statements from top to bottom.

steps.title: Trace the count
steps.text: Read the example before running it. console.log(value) prints the current value on its own line. The + between two numbers adds them. On a line such as open = open + 1, calculate the right side first.

steps.title: Run the board
steps.text: Run the example and compare each printed line with your prediction. The first line of output shows the opening count. The next print sees the updated open count. Assigning open a new value leaves opening at 4. For numbers, subtraction uses -. For text, + joins the pieces in order. In the second example the spaces inside the quotes become part of the label.

steps.title: Predict a type error
steps.text: TypeScript uses the initial value to work out a type (inference). In let count = 4, count can hold another number. Writing : number after the name would state the type explicitly (an annotation). Quoted digits are text. Look at the marked error example before you check it.

steps.title: Read the diagnostic
steps.text: Check the marked file. TS2322 is the compiler’s way of saying the value on the right has a type the name on the left cannot hold. The checker stops before running this answer. At runtime JavaScript uses the values themselves. In the label example it joins strings. A type annotation would not convert quoted digits into a number.

steps.title: Update a delivery
steps.text: Read the supplied opening and change values above the editor. Each check can supply different values. An input declaration such as const opening: number = 6 supplies a number you can read. Edit the starter, save, and compare both prints.

steps.title: Write two small answers
steps.text: Work from the prompt, then save each answer. One computes a changing number. The other constructs a fixed text label.

steps.title: Repair a broken count
steps.text: Read the compiler message before editing. Trace the value in the starter back to the line that gave it its type.

questions.prompt: What are the two output lines, in order?

choices.feedback: The first print runs before the assignment, the second after it.
The later assignment cannot change a line that has already printed.
open is a separate variable and receives the new number.

questions.prompt: What happens when the Practice Range checker checks this file?

choices.feedback: The checker checks types before running the file, and there is no print call.

choices.text: It converts the text to a number.
It reports an error on the assignment.
choices.feedback: count was inferred as number. The quotes make the new value a string.

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter after Functions, with the prior answer closed. A first unaided pass on both counts is later evidence of tracing and arithmetic. A hinted pass remains assisted.

drillGap: These drills isolate declaration forms. They do not check a snapshot against changing supplied input pairs.
